nodes.name: Generalized Fermat curve / group / pair of type $(k,n)$
nodes.statement: A closed Riemann surface $S$ is a called a generalized Fermat curve of the type $(k,n)$, where $k,n \geq 2$ are integers, if it admits a group $H \cong {\mathbb Z}_{k}^{n}$ of conformal automorphisms so that the quotient orbifold $S/H$ has genus zero and exactly $(n+1)$ conical points, each one necessarily of order $k$. In this case, the group $H$ (respectively, the pair $(S,H)$) is called a generalized Fermat group (respectively, a generalized Fermat pair) of type $(k,n)$.
nodes.statement_short: A closed Riemann surface admitting a ${\mathbb Z}_k^n$ action whose quotient orbifold is a genus-zero sphere with $n+1$ cone points of order $k$.
nodes.definiendum: generalized Fermat curve of the type $(k,n)$
differentia: it admits a group $H \cong {\mathbb Z}_{k}^{n}$ of conformal automorphisms so that the quotient orbifold $S/H$ has genus zero and exactly $(n+1)$ conical points, each one necessarily of order $k$

nodes.name: Genus $g_{k,n}$ of a generalized Fermat curve
nodes.statement: As a consequence of the Riemann-Hurwitz formula, it can be seen that $S$ has genus $$g_{k,n}:=\frac{k^{n-1}((n-1)(k-1)-2)+2}{2}.$$
nodes.statement_short: Riemann-Hurwitz gives the genus of a type-$(k,n)$ generalized Fermat curve in closed form.

nodes.name: Uniqueness of the generalized Fermat group
nodes.statement: In \cite{FGHL13} it was proved that, for $n=3$ and $k \geq 3$, a generalized Fermat curve of the type $(k,n)$ has a unique generalized Fermat group of type $(k,n)$ and later, in \cite{HKLP16}, as long $(k-1)(n-1)>2$ (equivalently, $g_{k,n}>1$), this uniqueness property was proved to be true in general.
nodes.statement_short: A generalized Fermat curve carries only one generalized Fermat group of its type once $(k-1)(n-1)>2$.
nodes.origin_citation: Fuertes, González-Diez, Hidalgo & Leyton-Álvarez 2013; Hidalgo, Kontogeorgis, Leyton-Álvarez & Paramantzoglou 2016
conclusions: a generalized Fermat curve of the type $(k,n)$ has a unique generalized Fermat group of type $(k,n)$

nodes.name: Identification of the moduli space of generalized Fermat curves
nodes.statement: This fact asserts that the moduli space of generalized Fermat curves of the type $(k,n)$ can be identified with the moduli space of orbifolds of genus zero with $(n+1)$ cone points, each one of order $k$. In particular, generalized Fermat curves of type $(k,n)$ provide a $(n-2)$ complex dimensional family inside the moduli space of surfaces of genus $g_{k,n}$ (those of type $(k,2)$ are exactly the classic Fermat curves of degree $k$).
nodes.statement_short: Uniqueness identifies $\mathcal{F}(k,n)$ with the moduli of $(n+1)$-punctured spheres, an $(n-2)$-dimensional family in ${\mathcal M}_{g_{k,n}}$.
assumptions: a generalized Fermat curve of the type $(k,n)$ has a unique generalized Fermat group of type $(k,n)$
conclusions: the moduli space of generalized Fermat curves of the type $(k,n)$ can be identified with the moduli space of orbifolds of genus zero with $(n+1)$ cone points, each one of order $k$

nodes.name: Uniformization of $(S,H)$ by the derived subgroup $\Gamma'$
nodes.statement: if the orbifold $S/H$ is uniformized by the Fuchsian group $\Gamma \cong\langle x_1,...,x_{n+1}: x_1^k=\cdots x_{n+1}^k=x_1\cdots x_{n+1}=1\rangle$, then its derived subgroup $\Gamma'$ is torsion free, it uniformizes $S$ and $H$ corresponds to $\Gamma/\Gamma'$. This, in particular, asserts that $S$ is a maximal Abelian branched covering space of the orbifold $S/H$.
nodes.statement_short: If $\Gamma$ uniformizes $S/H$ then $\Gamma'$ is torsion free, uniformizes $S$, and $H=\Gamma/\Gamma'$, so $S\to S/H$ is maximal Abelian.
assumptions: if the orbifold $S/H$ is uniformized by the Fuchsian group $\Gamma \cong\langle x_1,...,x_{n+1}: x_1^k=\cdots x_{n+1}^k=x_1\cdots x_{n+1}=1\rangle$
conclusions: its derived subgroup $\Gamma'$ is torsion free, it uniformizes $S$ and $H$ corresponds to $\Gamma/\Gamma'$

nodes.name: Algebraic model $\C{k}{n-2}{\lambda}$ of a generalized Fermat pair
nodes.statement: Then, $(S,H)$ is isomorphic to the pair $(\C{k}{n}{\lambda},H)$ (by abuse of notation we use $H$ in both contexts), where \begin{equation} \C{k}{n-2}{\lambda}:=\left \{ \begin{array}{rcc} x_0^k+x_1^k+x_2^k&=&0\\ \lambda_1x_0^k+x_1^k+x_3^k&=&0\\ \vdots \hspace{1cm}&\vdots &\vdots\\ \lambda_{n-2}x_0^k+x_1^k+x_n^k&=&0\\ \end{array}\right \}\subset {\mathbb{P}}^n, \end{equation} and $H$ is generated by the restrictions of the linear transformations \begin{center} $\varphi_j([x_0:\cdots:x_j:\cdots:x_n]):=[x_0:\cdots:w_kx_j:\cdots:x_n]$, where $w_k:={\mathrm{e}}^{\frac{2\pi i}{k}}$. \end{center}
nodes.statement_short: Every generalized Fermat pair is the fibre product of Fermat-type equations in ${\mathbb P}^n$ with $H$ generated by coordinate multiplications by $w_k$.

nodes.name: The set $F={\mathrm{Fix}}\;H$ of fixed points
nodes.statement: The set of fixed points of $\varphi_j$ in $\C{k}{n-2}{\lambda}$ is ${\mathrm{Fix}}(\varphi_j):=F_j \cap \C{k}{n-2}{\lambda}$, where $F_j$ is the hyperplane $\{x_j:=0\}\subset {\mathbb{P}}^n$. Set $F:=\cup_{j=0}^n{\mathrm{Fix}}(\varphi_j)={\mathrm{Fix}}\;H$.
nodes.statement_short: $F$ is the union of the fixed-point sets of the generators $\varphi_j$, cut out on the curve by the hyperplanes $\{x_j=0\}$.

nodes.name: Standard embedding of the generalized Fermat curve $S$
nodes.statement: The above produces an analytic embedding $S \hookrightarrow \C{k}{n-2}{\lambda} \subset {\mathbb{P}}^n$, called the standard embedding of the generalized Fermat curve $S$.
nodes.definiendum: standard embedding of the generalized Fermat curve $S$

nodes.name: Hyperosculating points of the standard embedding are the points of $F$
nodes.statement: In \cite{HKLP16} it was observed that the set hyperosculating points of such standard embeddings is $F$; in particular, these are Weierstrass points of $S$.
nodes.statement_short: The hyperosculating points of the standard embedding coincide with $F$, hence are Weierstrass points.
assumptions: the set hyperosculating points of such standard embeddings
conclusions: is $F$
these are Weierstrass points of $S$

nodes.name: Leopoldt's new Weierstrass points of the Fermat curve
nodes.statement: Leopoldt observed that for $k\geq 5$ the points $[1:\alpha: \sqrt[k]{2}\beta], [1:\sqrt[k]{2}\beta:\alpha]$ and $ [\sqrt[k]{2}:\beta: \alpha\beta]$, were $\alpha$ (resp. $\beta$) is a $k$-th root of $1$ (resp. $-1$) are $3k^2$ new Weierstrass points of the Fermat curve (for more information see Rohrlich's article \cite{Roh82}).
nodes.statement_short: For $k\ge5$ the Fermat curve has $3k^2$ further Weierstrass points beyond the hyperosculating ones.
conclusions: the points $[1:\alpha: \sqrt[k]{2}\beta], [1:\sqrt[k]{2}\beta:\alpha]$ and $ [\sqrt[k]{2}:\beta: \alpha\beta]$, were $\alpha$ (resp. $\beta$) is a $k$-th root of $1$ (resp. $-1$) are $3k^2$ new Weierstrass points of the Fermat curve

nodes.name: Additional Weierstrass points for $k=6$
nodes.statement: In 1999 Watanabe \cite{Wat99} showed that in the case $k=6$ additional Weierstrass points exist.
conclusions: additional Weierstrass points exist

nodes.name: Determination of all Weierstrass points and their weights
nodes.statement: The Weierstrass points are important in the geometry of Riemann surfaces, and in general the determination of all these points together their respective weights remains a difficult problem, including for classically known curves.
nodes.statement_short: Determining every Weierstrass point of a curve together with its weight is open even for classical curves.

nodes.name: The locus $\mathcal{F}(k,n)$ of generalized Fermat curves
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{F}(k,n)$ be the locus, in the moduli space ${\mathcal M}_{g_{k,n}}$ of curves of genus $g_{k,n}$, formed by all the (classes) of generalized Fermat curves of type $(k,n)$.
nodes.genus: the locus, in the moduli space ${\mathcal M}_{g_{k,n}}$ of curves of genus $g_{k,n}$
differentia: formed by all the (classes) of generalized Fermat curves of type $(k,n)$

nodes.name: $\mathcal{F}(k,n)\cong \mathcal{M}_{0,n+1}$
nodes.statement: The space $\mathcal{F}(k,n)$ is isomorphic to the moduli space $\mathcal{M}_{0,n+1}$ of the unordered $(n+1)$ punctured sphere (see section $4.2$ of \cite{GHL09}).
conclusions: The space $\mathcal{F}(k,n)$ is isomorphic to the moduli space $\mathcal{M}_{0,n+1}$ of the unordered $(n+1)$ punctured sphere

nodes.name: The parameter domain $\mathcal{P}_n$
nodes.statement: Let us consider the affine variety (in fact, a domain in ${\mathbb C}^{n-2}$) $$\mathcal{P}_n:=\{(\lambda_1,...,\lambda_{n-2})\in \mbox{(${\mathbb{C}}-\{0,1\}$)}^{n-2}\mid \lambda_i\neq \lambda_j\} \subset {\mathbb C}^{n-2}.$$
nodes.genus: the affine variety (in fact, a domain in ${\mathbb C}^{n-2}$)

nodes.name: Action of ${\mathfrak S}_{n+1}$ on ${\mathcal P}_{n}$
nodes.statement: To each $(\lambda_1,...,\lambda_{n-2})\in \mathcal{P}_n$ we associate the $(n+1)$-tuple $(\gamma_1,\gamma_2,\gamma_3,\gamma_4,...,\gamma_{n+1})=(\infty, 0,1,\lambda_1,...,\lambda_{n-2})$. Given an element $\sigma \in \mathfrak{S}_{n+1}$, the permutation group of $n+1$ elements, we can form the $(n+1)$-tuple $(\gamma_{\sigma^{-1}(1)},\gamma_{\sigma^{-1}(2)},...,\gamma_{\sigma^{-1}(n+1)})$. Let $T_{\sigma}\in {\rm PSL}(2,\mathbb{C})$ be the unique M\"obius Transformation satisfying $T_{\sigma}(\gamma_{\sigma^{-1}(1)})=\infty$, $T_{\sigma}(\gamma_{\sigma^{-1}(2)})=0$, and $T_{\sigma}(\gamma_{\sigma^{-1}(3)})=1$, and set $$\sigma \cdot (\lambda_{1},\ldots, \lambda_{n-2})=(T_{\sigma} (\gamma_{\sigma^{-1}(4)}),...,T_{\sigma} (\gamma_{\sigma^{-1}(n+1)}) \in {\mathcal P}_{n}.$$ The above provides an action of ${\mathfrak S}_{n+1}$ as a group of holomorphic automorphisms on ${\mathcal P}_{n}$ $$ \mathfrak{S}_{n+1}\times \mathcal{P}_n\rightarrow \mathcal{P}_n; (\lambda_{1},\ldots, \lambda_{n-2})\mapsto \sigma \cdot (\lambda_{1},\ldots, \lambda_{n-2}). $$
nodes.statement_short: Permuting the $(n+1)$ branch values and renormalizing by the Möbius map $T_\sigma$ defines a holomorphic ${\mathfrak S}_{n+1}$-action on ${\mathcal P}_n$.

nodes.name: Faithfulness of the ${\mathfrak S}_{n+1}$-action
nodes.statement: The above action is faithful for $n \geq 4$. For $n=3$ there is a subgroup isomorphic to ${\mathbb Z}_{2}^{2}$ acting trivially on ${\mathcal P}_{3}$.
conclusions: The above action is faithful
there is a subgroup isomorphic to ${\mathbb Z}_{2}^{2}$ acting trivially on ${\mathcal P}_{3}$

nodes.name: Isomorphism criterion for generalized Fermat curves
nodes.statement: In \cite{GHL09} it was observed that two generalized Fermat curves $\C{k}{n-2}{\lambda}$ and $\C{k}{n-2}{\mu}$ are isomorphic if and only if $(\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{n-2})$ and $(\mu_{1},\ldots,\mu_{n-2})$ are in the same ${\mathfrak S}_{n+1}$-orbit.
nodes.statement_short: Two generalized Fermat curves are isomorphic exactly when their parameter tuples lie in one ${\mathfrak S}_{n+1}$-orbit.
conclusions: are isomorphic if and only if $(\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{n-2})$ and $(\mu_{1},\ldots,\mu_{n-2})$ are in the same ${\mathfrak S}_{n+1}$-orbit

nodes.name: $\mathcal{F}(k,n)$ as the geometric quotient $\mathcal{P}_n/\mathfrak{S}_{n+1}$
nodes.statement: This, in particular, permits us to realize the moduli space $\mathcal{F}(k,n)$ as a geometric quotient $\mathcal{P}_n/\mathfrak{S}_{n+1}$, that is, as a complex (affine) variety and that the canonical projection map $\Pi: \mathcal{P}_n\to \mathcal{P}_n /{\mathfrak S}_{n+1}$ is an open morphism.
nodes.statement_short: $\mathcal{F}(k,n)$ is the affine geometric quotient $\mathcal{P}_n/{\mathfrak S}_{n+1}$ and the projection $\Pi$ is open.
assumptions: two generalized Fermat curves $\C{k}{n-2}{\lambda}$ and $\C{k}{n-2}{\mu}$ are isomorphic if and only if $(\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{n-2})$ and $(\mu_{1},\ldots,\mu_{n-2})$ are in the same ${\mathfrak S}_{n+1}$-orbit
conclusions: realize the moduli space $\mathcal{F}(k,n)$ as a geometric quotient $\mathcal{P}_n/\mathfrak{S}_{n+1}$, that is, as a complex (affine) variety
the canonical projection map $\Pi: \mathcal{P}_n\to \mathcal{P}_n /{\mathfrak S}_{n+1}$ is an open morphism

nodes.name: Multiplicity of an $l$-plane $P$ at $p$
nodes.statement: Let $C \subset {\mathbb{P}}^n$ be a projective smooth curve. For a $l$-plane $P\subset {\mathbb{P}}^{n}$, $1\leq l\leq n-1$, the multiplicity of $P$ in $p$ is \begin{center} $\mult{P}{C}:=\mbox{Order of contact of $P$ and $C$ in $p$}$. \end{center}
nodes.genus: Order of contact of $P$ and $C$ in $p$

nodes.name: Existence and uniqueness of the osculating $l$-plane
nodes.statement: It is known that, for each $p \in C$, there exists a unique $l$-plane, called the {\it osculating $l$-plane} and denoted by $\osc{l}{p}$, such that $\mult{\osc{l}{p}}{C}\geq l+1$, and that there exists at most a finite number of points $p\in C$ such that $\mult{\osc{l}{p}}{C}> l+1$.
nodes.statement_short: Each point has a unique osculating $l$-plane meeting $C$ to order $\ge l+1$, and higher contact happens only finitely often.
conclusions: there exists a unique $l$-plane, called the {\it osculating $l$-plane} and denoted by $\osc{l}{p}$, such that $\mult{\osc{l}{p}}{C}\geq l+1$
there exists at most a finite number of points $p\in C$ such that $\mult{\osc{l}{p}}{C}> l+1$

nodes.name: Hyperosculating point
nodes.statement: We say that $p\in C$ is a hyperosculating point if $$\mult{\osc{n-1}{p}}{C}>n.$$

nodes.name: Hyperosculating points of a canonical embedding are the Weierstrass points
nodes.statement: If $C$ is a non hyperelliptic curve of genus $g \geq 3$, then the hyperosculating points of the canonical embedding of $C \hookrightarrow {\mathbb P}^{g-1}$ are exactly its Weierstrass points.

nodes.name: The maps $f_l:C\rightarrow \G{l+1}{n+1}$
nodes.statement: As the $l$-planes of ${\mathbb{P}}^n$ are in bijective correspondence with the dimension $(l+1)$ vector subspaces of ${\mathbb{C}}^{n+1}$, we can define the functions $$f_l:C\rightarrow \G{l+1}{n+1}; p\mapsto \osc{l}{p},$$ where $\G{l+1}{n+1}$ is the corresponding Grasmannian manifold.
nodes.statement_short: $f_l$ sends a point to its osculating $l$-plane, viewed in the Grassmannian of $(l+1)$-dimensional subspaces.

nodes.name: Associated curves $C_l$
nodes.statement: The curves $C_l:=f_l(C)$, $0\leq l\leq n-1$ are called the associated curves of $C$.

nodes.name: Local vectorial function $v(z)$ and its wedge $w(z)$
nodes.statement: Let $f_0:C\rightarrow {\mathbb{P}}^n$ be the natural embedding defined by the inclusion $C\subset {\mathbb{P}}^n$, and let us consider a local chart $z:U\subset C \rightarrow W \subset {\mathbb{C}} $, $z(p)=0$, around the point $p\in C$. Then there exists a neighborhood $W'\subset W$ of $0$, and a holomorphic vectorial function $$v:W'\rightarrow {\mathbb{C}}^{n+1}\backslash\{0\}:\;z \mapsto v(z):=(v_0(z),v_1(z),...,v_n(z)),$$ such that $$ f_0(z)=[v_0(z):v_1(z):\cdots:v_n(z)], \quad \mbox{for all $z\in W'$.} $$ Let us consider the holomorphic vectorial function $$w:W'\rightarrow \wedge^{l+1}{\mathbb{C}}^{n+1}:\; z\mapsto w(z):=v(z)\wedge v'(z)\wedge \cdots \wedge v^{(l)}(z).$$
nodes.statement_short: Choose a local lift $v(z)$ of the embedding and form the wedge of its first $l$ derivatives.

nodes.name: Plücker representation of $f_l$
nodes.statement: There exists an integer $m\geq 0$ such that $w(z)/z^{m}$ is a holomorphic vectorial function which does not vanish in a neighborhood $W''$ of $z=0$. By abuse of notation, we may say that $[w(z)]\in {\mathbb{P}}(\wedge^{l+1}{\mathbb{C}}^{n+1})$ for all $z\in W''$. Using the Pl\"ucker coordinates, it is possible to see $\G{l+1}{n+1}$ as a subvariety of ${\mathbb{P}}(\wedge^{l+1}{\mathbb{C}}^{n+1})$ and that $$ f_l(z)=[v(z)\wedge v^{'}(z)\wedge \cdots \wedge v^{(l)}(z) ], \quad \mbox{ for all $z\in W''$}. $$ In particular, the maps $f_l$ are holomorphic and independent of the parametrization $v(z)$ chosen.
nodes.statement_short: In Plücker coordinates $f_l(z)=[v\wedge v'\wedge\cdots\wedge v^{(l)}]$, so the $f_l$ are holomorphic and parametrization-independent.
assumptions: Using the Pl\"ucker coordinates, it is possible to see $\G{l+1}{n+1}$ as a subvariety of ${\mathbb{P}}(\wedge^{l+1}{\mathbb{C}}^{n+1})$
conclusions: the maps $f_l$ are holomorphic and independent of the parametrization $v(z)$ chosen

nodes.name: Ramification indexes $b_l(p)$, $b_l$ and the ranks $d_l$
nodes.statement: Let us define the following integers: \begin{itemize} \item $b_l(p)$; the ramification index of $f_l:C\rightarrow C_l$ in the point $p\in C$. \item $b_l=\sum_{p\in C}b_l(p)$; the total ramification index of $f_l:C\rightarrow C_l$. \item $d_l$; the number of osculating $l$-planes of $C$ which intersects a generic $(n-l-1)$-plane of ${\mathbb{P}}^{n}$. Observe that $d_0$ is simply the degree of the curve. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: $b_l(p)$ is the ramification index of $f_l$ at $p$, $b_l$ its total, and $d_l$ the number of osculating $l$-planes meeting a generic $(n-l-1)$-plane.

nodes.name: Characterization of hyperosculating points by ramification
nodes.statement: The point $p\in C\subset {\mathbb{P}}^n$ is a hyperosculating point if and only if $\sum_{l=1}^{n-1}b_l(p)\geq 1$.
conclusions: is a hyperosculating point if and only if $\sum_{l=1}^{n-1}b_l(p)\geq 1$

nodes.name: Plücker Formulas
nodes.statement: If $C\subset {\mathbb{P}}^n$ is a curve of genus $g$, then \begin{center} $d_{l+1}-2d_l+d_{l-1}=2g-2-b_l$, for all $1\leq l\leq n-1$, \end{center} where $d_{-1}=d_n=0$.
nodes.statement_short: The ranks $d_l$ of a genus-$g$ curve satisfy the second-order recursion $d_{l+1}-2d_l+d_{l-1}=2g-2-b_l$.
assumptions: If $C\subset {\mathbb{P}}^n$ is a curve of genus $g$
conclusions: $d_{l+1}-2d_l+d_{l-1}=2g-2-b_l$, for all $1\leq l\leq n-1$,
where $d_{-1}=d_n=0$

nodes.name: Normal form of $f_0$ at $p$
nodes.statement: Making linear changes of coordinates, it is possible to prove that there exists $\varphi\in {\mathrm{Aut}}({\mathbb{P}}^n)\cong \PGL{n+1}{{\mathbb{C}}}$ such that $$ \varphi(f_0(z))=[1: z^{1+\alpha_1}+\cdots: z^{2+\alpha_1+\alpha_2}+\cdots:\cdots :z^{n+\alpha_1+\cdots+\alpha_n}+\cdots]. $$ This is called the normal form of $f_0$ in $p$.
nodes.statement_short: After a projective change of coordinates the embedding reads $[1:z^{1+\alpha_1}+\cdots:\cdots:z^{n+\alpha_1+\cdots+\alpha_n}+\cdots]$.

nodes.name: Invariance of the exponents $\alpha_j$
nodes.statement: It is possible to verify that the integers $\alpha_j$, $1\leq j\leq n$, only depend on $f_0$ and the point $p\in C$, and neither on the chosen local chart $z$, nor the vectorial function $v(z)$, nor the automorphism $\varphi$.
conclusions: only depend on $f_0$ and the point $p\in C$, and neither on the chosen local chart $z$, nor the vectorial function $v(z)$, nor the automorphism $\varphi$

nodes.name: Ramification index equals the normal-form exponent
nodes.statement: In the above, $$ b_l(p):=\alpha_{l+1}, \quad 0\leq l\leq n-1. $$
conclusions: $$ b_l(p):=\alpha_{l+1}, \quad 0\leq l\leq n-1. $$

nodes.name: Gap values from the normal-form exponents
nodes.statement: If $C$ is a non-hyperelliptic curve of genus $g \geq 3$ and $C\hookrightarrow {\mathbb{P}}^{g-1}$ is a canonical embedding, then $$ a_i=i+\sum_{j=1}^{i-1}\alpha_j, \quad 1\leq i\leq g, $$ are the gap values of $p$. In other words, $a_{1},\ldots,a_{g}$ are the only $g$ integers where {\bf there does not exist} a meromorphic function of $C$ with a pole of order $a_i$ in the point $p$ and holomorphic on $C-\{p\}$.
nodes.statement_short: For a canonical embedding the gap values are $a_i=i+\sum_{j<i}\alpha_j$.

nodes.name: Restriction of a rational map to $\C{k}{n-2}{\lambda}$ is a morphism
nodes.statement: Let us consider a generalized Fermat curve of type $(k,n)$ with its respective standard embedding $\xymatrix{\C{k}{n-2}{\lambda} \ar@^{(->}[r] & {\mathbb{P}}^{n} }$, and a rational map (denoted by the dotted line) $\psi: {\mathbb{P}}^{n} \dashrightarrow {\mathbb{P}}^{m}$. If there exists $0 \leq i<j\leq n$ such that the linear projective space $L_{(i,j)}:=\{[x_0:\cdots:x_n]|x_i=x_j=0\}$ contains the locus of indeterminacy of the rational map, then (as the intersection $\C{k}{n-2}{\lambda}\cap L_{(i,j)}$ is the empty set) the restriction of $\psi$ to $\C{k}{n-2}{\lambda}$, $$\xymatrix{ \C{k}{n-2}{\lambda} \ar@^{(->}[r] \ar@/^1pc/[rr]&{\mathbb{P}}^{n}\ar@{-->}[r]&{\mathbb{P}}^m},$$ is a well defined morphism.
nodes.statement_short: If the indeterminacy locus of $\psi$ sits inside some $L_{(i,j)}$, then $\psi$ restricts to a morphism on the curve, since $\C{k}{n-2}{\lambda}\cap L_{(i,j)}=\emptyset$.
nodes.section: 2.4 The natural regular branched coverings of the generalized Fermat curves

nodes.name: The projection $\pi:{\mathbb{P}}^{n} \dashrightarrow {\mathbb{P}}^{n-1}$
nodes.statement: Let us consider the rational map $$\pi: {\mathbb{P}}^{n} \dashrightarrow {\mathbb{P}}^{n-1}: [x_0:\cdots:x_n] \mapsto [x_0:\cdots:x_{n-1}].$$
nodes.section: 2.4 The natural regular branched coverings of the generalized Fermat curves

nodes.name: $\pi$ restricts to a morphism $\C{k}{n-2}{\lambda}\to\C{k}{n-3}{\lambda}$
nodes.statement: As the locus of indeterminacy of $\pi$ is the point $[0:\cdots:0:1]\in L_{(0,1)} \subset {\mathbb{P}}^{n}$, then (by Remark \ref{re:rest}) the restriction of $\pi$ to $\C{k}{n-2}{\lambda}$ is a well defined morphism. Additionally, $\pi(\C{k}{n-2}{\lambda}))=\C{k}{n-3}{\lambda}$ (when $n=3$, this image curve is the classic Fermat curve $C^k$).
nodes.statement_short: Because the indeterminacy point of $\pi$ lies in $L_{(0,1)}$, $\pi$ restricts to a morphism onto the type-$(k,n-1)$ curve.
nodes.section: 2.4 The natural regular branched coverings of the generalized Fermat curves
assumptions: the locus of indeterminacy of $\pi$ is the point $[0:\cdots:0:1]\in L_{(0,1)} \subset {\mathbb{P}}^{n}$
conclusions: the restriction of $\pi$ to $\C{k}{n-2}{\lambda}$ is a well defined morphism
$\pi(\C{k}{n-2}{\lambda}))=\C{k}{n-3}{\lambda}$

nodes.name: $\pi$ is a regular branched covering with deck group $\langle\varphi_n\rangle$
nodes.statement: Note that the restricted map $\pi$, is a regular branched covering whose deck covering group is the cyclic group generated the automorphism $$\varphi_n([x_0:\cdots:x_n]):=[x_0:\cdots :\mathrm{e}^{\frac{2\pi i}{k}}x_n],$$ so its branch values are the images of the $k^{n-1}$ fixed points of $\varphi_{n}$. This map $\pi$ is compatible with the embeddings of the Fermat curves into projective spaces. The quotient group $H/\langle \varphi_{n}\rangle \cong {\mathbb Z}_{k}^{n-1}$ is the generalized Fermat group of type $(k,n-1)$ of $\C{k}{n-3}{\lambda}$. The $k^{n-1}$ fixed points of each $\varphi_{j}$ ($j=0,\ldots,n$) are permuted under the action of $\varphi_{n}$ (fixing none of them), and this set is projected under $\pi$ to the set of $k^{n-2}$ fixed points of the quotient class of $\varphi_{j}$.
nodes.statement_short: $\pi$ is the cyclic degree-$k$ cover given by $\varphi_n$; its branch values are the images of the $k^{n-1}$ fixed points, and $H/\langle\varphi_n\rangle$ is the generalized Fermat group downstairs.

nodes.statement: If $p \in F$, then, by using linear substitutions in the system of equations, we may assume that $p\in {\mathrm{Fix}}(\varphi_1)$, that is, $$p:=[1:0:\rho_1:\rho_2:\cdots:\rho_{n-1}],$$ where $\rho_i^{k}=-{\lambda}_{i-1}$, $1\leq i\leq n-1$ (with ${\lambda}_{0}=1$).

nodes.statement: \begin{enumerate} \item The set of hyperosculating points of $\C{k}{n-2}{\lambda}$ is $F$. \item If $p\in F$, then $b_1(p)=k-2$ and $b_l(p)=k-1$, $l \in \{2,\ldots, n-1\}$. \end{enumerate}

nodes.statement: Let $z$ be a local chart of $\C{k}{n-2}{\lambda}$ around the point $p\in \C{k}{n-2}{\lambda}$. nodes.name: Proof that $x_0^{r-j}$ and $x_1^{r-j}$ are independent in $Q(r-j)$

nodes.statement: If $s(r-j):= \dim_{{\mathbb{C}}}Q(r-j)$, where $r:=(n-1)(k-1)-2$ and $0\leq j\leq k-1$, then $$s(r-j)=\frac{1}{2} k^{n-2} ((n(k-1) -2 - 2 j)+ \delta_{k-1, j},$$ where $\delta_{k-1, j}$ is the Kronecker delta.

nodes.name: Proof of the dimension formula for $Q(r-j)$
nodes.statement: Let us fix a generalized Fermat curve $\C{k}{n-2}{\lambda}$, and consider the generalized Fermat curve $S'=\C{k}{n-3}{\lambda}$ of type $(n-1,k)$. We note that $$H^{0}(S',\mathcal{O}_{S'}(r-j))\cong Q(r-j).$$ For $m\in{\mathbb{Z}}$, let $h'(m)$ denote the dimension of the global section space $H^{0}(S',\mathcal{O}_{S'}(m))$ over ${\mathbb{C}}$. Recall that $\omega_{S'}\cong \mathcal{O}_{S'}((n-2)(k-1)-2)$. By the Riemann-Roch Formula, $$h'(-k+1+j))-h'(r'-(-k+1+j))=(-k+1+j)k^{n-2}-\left(\frac{k^{n-2} r' +2}{2}\right)+1,$$ where $r':=(n-2)(k-1)-2$. Since $s(r-j)= h'(r'-(-k+1+j))$ and $h'(-k+1+j))=\delta_{k-1, j}$, we obtain the desired equality.
nodes.statement_short: Identify $Q(r-j)$ with global sections on the quotient curve $S'$ and apply Riemann-Roch there.

nodes.name: Optimal lower bound for the Weierstrass weight of the points of $F$
nodes.statement: Let $p \in F$ and let $w(p)$ be its weight. If $n\geq 3$, then $$\widehat{w}(p):=\frac{1}{24}(k-1) (k^{n-1}-2) (k^{n} + k^{n-1}-12)\leq w(p).$$ Moreover, there exists a dense open set of $\mathcal{F}(k,n)$ where equality holds.
nodes.statement_short: For $n\ge3$ the weight of any $p\in F$ is at least $\widehat{w}(p)=\tfrac1{24}(k-1)(k^{n-1}-2)(k^n+k^{n-1}-12)$, with equality on a dense open subset of moduli.

nodes.name: The classic Fermat curve case $(k,2)$
nodes.statement: In the case of a generalized Fermat curve of the type $(k,2)$, $k\geq 4$, (a classic Fermat curve), it is known that (see \cite{Has50,Roh82,Wat99}) the weight of a point $p\in F$ is $w(p)=\frac{1}{24}(k-1)(k-2)(k-3)(k+4)$, which shows that equality in Theorem \ref{th:w-peso} holds for the classic case.
nodes.statement_short: For classic Fermat curves the known weight $\frac1{24}(k-1)(k-2)(k-3)(k+4)$ matches the bound.

nodes.name: Generalized Fermat curve of type $(2,4)$
nodes.statement: Let $C$ be a generalized Fermat curve of the type $(k,n)=(2,4)$, and $p$ be in $F$. As $H^{0}(C,\omega_C)\cong H^{0}(C,\mathcal{O}_C(1))={\mathbb{C}}[x_0,x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4]_1$ (forms of degree $1$ of the polynomial ring ${\mathbb{C}}[x_0,x_1,x_2,x_3]$), It follows that the map $\xymatrix{ C \ar[r]^{f_c}&{\mathbb{P}}^{4}}$ is the canonical embedding. Using the normal form of $f_{c}$ in $p$, we obtain that the gap values of $p$ are $a_1=1$, $a_2=2$, $a_3=3$, $a_4=5$, $a_5=7$. In this way, $\hat{w}(p)=w(p)=3$. Observe that, by virtue of Theorem \ref{th:hyperosc}, in this case the Weierstrass points are exactly the points of hyperosculation $F$.
nodes.statement_short: For type $(2,4)$ the gaps are $1,2,3,5,7$, so $\hat{w}(p)=w(p)=3$ and the bound is attained.

nodes.name: Generalized Fermat curve $C^5(-1)$ of type $(5,3)$
nodes.statement: Consider the following generalized Fermat curve of the type $(5,3)$ \begin{center} $C^5(-1):=\left \{ \begin{array}{rcc} x_0^5+x_1^5+x_2^5&=&0\\ -x_0^5+x_1^5+x_3^5&=&0 \end{array}\right .$ \end{center} and $p=[1:1:-\sqrt[5]{2}:0]$. In this case, $\hat{w}(p)<w(p)$. In Section \ref{Sec:finalejemplo} we provide a proof of this fact.
nodes.statement_short: For $C^5(-1)$ and $p=[1:1:-\sqrt[5]{2}:0]$ the bound is strict: $\hat{w}(p)<w(p)$.
nodes.section: 3.1 The Weierstrass weight of the hyperosculating points of generalized Fermat curves

nodes.name: Reduction to $n\geq 3$ and normalization of $p$ in the proof
nodes.statement: Because of Example \ref{ej:cla-fer}, we only need to consider $n\geq 3$. Let us consider the generalized Fermat curve $\C{k}{n-2}{\lambda}$, and $p\in F$. Without loss of generality, we can suppose that $p:=[1:\rho_1:\rho_2:\cdots :\rho_{n-1}:0]$, where $\rho_i^k=-\lambda_{n-2}-\lambda_{i-2}$, $\lambda_{-1}=0$, and $\lambda_{0}=1$ (it suffices to use the linear substitutions in the system of equations $\C{k}{n-2}{\lambda}$). Also, let us recall the commutative diagram \eqref{diagrama2}.
nodes.statement_short: Only $n\ge3$ remains, and $p$ may be normalized to $[1:\rho_1:\cdots:\rho_{n-1}:0]$.

nodes.name: The sets $\mho_j$ and $\mho$ of good parameters
nodes.statement: The set $D(\lambda_1,...,\lambda_{n-2})=\pi({\mathrm{Fix}}(\varphi_n))\subset \C{k}{n-3}{\lambda}$, is the set of branch values of the regular branched covering map $\pi:\C{k}{n-2}{\lambda} \to \C{k}{n-3}{\lambda}$ whose deck group is $\langle \phi_{n} \rangle \cong {\mathbb Z}_{k}$. Define the sets $$\mho_j:=\{(\lambda_1,...\lambda_{n-2})\in\mathcal{M}_{0, n+1} \mid D(\lambda_1,...,\lambda_{n-2}) \cap \HC{j}{k}{n-3}{\lambda}=\emptyset \},$$ $$\mho:=\cap_{j=0}^{k-1}\mho_{j},$$ where $\HC{j}{k}{n-3}{\lambda}$ is the set of hyperosculating points of the map $$g_j:\C{k}{n-3}{\lambda}\hookrightarrow {\mathbb{P}}(Q(r-j)).$$
nodes.statement_short: $\mho_j$ collects the moduli where the branch values of $\pi$ avoid the hyperosculating points of $g_j$, and $\mho$ is their intersection.

nodes.name: $\mho_j$ is a dense open set
nodes.statement: For each $j \in \{0,\ldots,k-1\}$, the set $\mho_j$ is a dense open set of $\mathcal{M}_{0,n}$; in particular, $\mho$ is also a non-empty dense open set.
conclusions: the set $\mho_j$ is a dense open set of $\mathcal{M}_{0,n}$
$\mho$ is also a non-empty dense open set

nodes.name: Proof that $\mho_j$ is dense open
nodes.statement: Let us consider the set $$\mho'_j:=\{(\lambda_1,...\lambda_{n-2})\in\mathcal{P}_n \mid D(\lambda_1,..., \lambda_{n-2})\cap \HC{j}{k}{n-3}{\lambda}=\emptyset \}.$$ As $\Pi: \mho'_j\rightarrow \mho_j$ is an open surjective map (see section \ref{sec:pre-mod-esp}), it suffices to prove that $\mho'_j$ is an open set in the domain ${\mathcal P}_{n} \subset {\mathbb C}^{n-2}$. In the following, when we use the notation $\hat{\lambda}_i$ we suppose that the value of $\lambda_i$ is fixed. Let us first verify that $\mho'_j$ is non-empty. Fix a point $(\hat{\lambda}_1,...,\hat{\lambda}_{n-3}) \in {\mathcal P}_{n-1}$ and consider the slice in ${\mathcal P}_{n}$ given by the points of the form $(\hat{\lambda}_1,...,\hat{\lambda}_{n-3}, \lambda_{n-2}) \in {\mathcal P}_{n}$. We proceed to see that in such a slice only finitely many points cannot belong to $\mho_{j}$. For it, we only need to observe that $$\{q:=\pi(p)\in \C{k}{n-3}{\hat{\lambda}}\mid \lambda_{n-2}\in {\mathbb{C}}-\{0,1, \hat{\lambda}_1,...,\hat{\lambda}_{n-3} \},\; p\in {\mathrm{Fix}}{(\varphi_n)}\}$$ has infinitely many points and $\HC{j}{k}{n-3}{\hat{\lambda}}$ is a finite set. Now, we proceed to check that $\mho'_{j}$ is open. Let us fix $(\hat{\lambda}_0,...,\hat{\lambda}_{n-2}) \in \mho'_{j}$. Let $q'\in D(\hat{\lambda}_0,...,\hat{\lambda}_{n-3})$ be such that $q'\not\in \HC{j}{k}{n-3}{\hat{\lambda}}$ and $p'\in {\mathrm{Fix}}{(\varphi_n)}$ such that $\pi(p')=q'$. For each $(\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{n-2}) \in {\mathcal P}_{n}$, let us consider a point $p\in {\mathrm{Fix}}{(\varphi_{n})}\subset \C{k}{n-2}{\lambda}$ and set $q=\pi(p)$. Observe that there are no technical problems in supposing that $(p,q)=(p',q')$ when $(\lambda_{1},\cdots, \lambda_{n-2})=(\hat{\lambda}_{1},\cdots, \hat{\lambda}_{n-2})$. Recall that we may assume $p=[1:\rho_1:\cdots :\rho_{n-1}:0]$, where $\rho_i^k=-\lambda_{n-2}-\lambda_{i-2}$, $\lambda_{-1}=0$ and $\lambda_{0}=1$. If $z$ is a local chart around $p$, $z(p)=0$, then there exists a neighborhood $\Omega_p \subset {\mathbb{C}}$ of $0$, such that the map $f_0:\Omega_p \rightarrow \C{k}{n-2}{\lambda}\subset {\mathbb{P}}^{n}$, defined naturally by the embedding $\C{k}{n-2}{\lambda}\subset {\mathbb{P}}^{n}$, has the form $$ \displaystyle f_0(z)=[1:h_1(z^{k}):h_2(z^{k}): \cdots: h_{n-1}(z^{k}):z],$$ where $h_i(0)=\rho_{i}$. By the construction, there exists a local chart $\zeta$ of $\C{k}{n-3}{\lambda}$ around the point $q:=\pi(p)$, and a local parametrization $$\tilde{f}_0:\Omega'_q\subset {\mathbb{C}}\rightarrow \C{k}{n-3}{\lambda}\subset {\mathbb{P}}^{n-1}:\zeta\mapsto \tilde{f}_0(\zeta)=[1:h_1(\zeta):h_2(\zeta): \cdots: h_{n-1}(\zeta)].$$ Recall that the morphism $\pi$ is defined in local charts as $\zeta=\pi(z)=z^k$. Additionally, if we consider a Taylor expansion of the $h_i(\zeta)$ we can observe that the coefficients are analytic functions in the variables $\lambda_1,...,\lambda_{n-2}$. Now let us consider the map $g_{j}:\C{k}{n-3}{\lambda}\rightarrow {\mathbb{P}}(Q(r-j))$. We note that, using the local parametrization of $\tilde{f}_0(\zeta)$ around the point $q$, a local parametrization of $g_{j}$ around the point $q$ can be found. Let $g_{j}(\zeta):=[1:h'_1(\zeta):\cdots:h'_{t_j}(\zeta)]$ be this local parametrization of $g_{j}$, where $t_j:=s(r-j)-1= \dim_{{\mathbb{C}}}Q(r-j)-1$. By construction the coefficients of $h'_i(\zeta)$ are analytic functions in the variables $\lambda_1,...,\lambda_{n-2}$. Given a formal series $l(\zeta)$, let $Tl$ be the vector column formed by all the coefficients of the formal series $l(\zeta)$ until the grade $t_j$. We consider the following analytic function defined over $\mathcal{P}_n$ $$r(\lambda_1,...,\lambda_{n-2})=\det(T1,Th'_1,...,Th'_{t_j}).$$ Fixing the values $\lambda_1,...,\lambda_{n-2}$, the point $q\in \C{k}{n-3}{\lambda}$ is not a point of $\HC{j}{k}{n-3}{\lambda}$ if and only if $r(\lambda_1,...,\lambda_{n-2})$ is not zero. As $q'$ is not a point of $\HC{j}{k}{n-3}{\hat{\lambda}}$, we have that $r(\hat{\lambda}_1,...,\hat{\lambda}_{n-2})\neq 0$ (in particular, $r$ is not identically zero). The set $\mho'_j\subset \mathcal{P}_n$, where the analytic function $r$ does not vanish, is the sought after open set.
nodes.statement_short: Lift to $\mho'_j\subset\mathcal{P}_n$ using openness of $\Pi$, then exhibit an analytic determinant $r(\lambda)$ whose non-vanishing locus is exactly $\mho'_j$.

nodes.name: Lift $\mho_j$ to $\mho'_j\subset\mathcal{P}_n$
nodes.statement: Let us consider the set $$\mho'_j:=\{(\lambda_1,...\lambda_{n-2})\in\mathcal{P}_n \mid D(\lambda_1,..., \lambda_{n-2})\cap \HC{j}{k}{n-3}{\lambda}=\emptyset \}.$$
nodes.statement_short: Define the pre-image $\mho'_j$ of $\mho_j$ inside the parameter domain.

nodes.name: Reduce to openness of $\mho'_j$ via the open surjection $\Pi$
nodes.statement: As $\Pi: \mho'_j\rightarrow \mho_j$ is an open surjective map (see section \ref{sec:pre-mod-esp}), it suffices to prove that $\mho'_j$ is an open set in the domain ${\mathcal P}_{n} \subset {\mathbb C}^{n-2}$.
nodes.statement_short: Because $\Pi$ is open and surjective, it is enough to work upstairs in $\mathcal{P}_n$.

nodes.name: Notation for fixed parameters $\hat{\lambda}_i$
nodes.statement: In the following, when we use the notation $\hat{\lambda}_i$ we suppose that the value of $\lambda_i$ is fixed.
nodes.statement_short: Hats mark the coordinates that are held fixed.

nodes.name: Non-emptiness of $\mho'_j$ via a slice
nodes.statement: Let us first verify that $\mho'_j$ is non-empty. Fix a point $(\hat{\lambda}_1,...,\hat{\lambda}_{n-3}) \in {\mathcal P}_{n-1}$ and consider the slice in ${\mathcal P}_{n}$ given by the points of the form $(\hat{\lambda}_1,...,\hat{\lambda}_{n-3}, \lambda_{n-2}) \in {\mathcal P}_{n}$. We proceed to see that in such a slice only finitely many points cannot belong to $\mho_{j}$. For it, we only need to observe that $$\{q:=\pi(p)\in \C{k}{n-3}{\hat{\lambda}}\mid \lambda_{n-2}\in {\mathbb{C}}-\{0,1, \hat{\lambda}_1,...,\hat{\lambda}_{n-3} \},\; p\in {\mathrm{Fix}}{(\varphi_n)}\}$$ has infinitely many points and $\HC{j}{k}{n-3}{\hat{\lambda}}$ is a finite set.
nodes.statement_short: On a slice with all but one parameter fixed, infinitely many branch points meet a finite hyperosculating set, so only finitely many parameters fail.

nodes.name: Fix a base point of $\mho'_j$ and a non-hyperosculating branch value
nodes.statement: Now, we proceed to check that $\mho'_{j}$ is open. Let us fix $(\hat{\lambda}_0,...,\hat{\lambda}_{n-2}) \in \mho'_{j}$. Let $q'\in D(\hat{\lambda}_0,...,\hat{\lambda}_{n-3})$ be such that $q'\not\in \HC{j}{k}{n-3}{\hat{\lambda}}$ and $p'\in {\mathrm{Fix}}{(\varphi_n)}$ such that $\pi(p')=q'$.
nodes.statement_short: Pick $\hat\lambda\in\mho'_j$, a branch value $q'\notin \HC{j}{k}{n-3}{\hat{\lambda}}$ and $p'$ above it.

nodes.name: Local parametrization of $f_0$ near $p$
nodes.statement: For each $(\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{n-2}) \in {\mathcal P}_{n}$, let us consider a point $p\in {\mathrm{Fix}}{(\varphi_{n})}\subset \C{k}{n-2}{\lambda}$ and set $q=\pi(p)$. Observe that there are no technical problems in supposing that $(p,q)=(p',q')$ when $(\lambda_{1},\cdots, \lambda_{n-2})=(\hat{\lambda}_{1},\cdots, \hat{\lambda}_{n-2})$. Recall that we may assume $p=[1:\rho_1:\cdots :\rho_{n-1}:0]$, where $\rho_i^k=-\lambda_{n-2}-\lambda_{i-2}$, $\lambda_{-1}=0$ and $\lambda_{0}=1$. If $z$ is a local chart around $p$, $z(p)=0$, then there exists a neighborhood $\Omega_p \subset {\mathbb{C}}$ of $0$, such that the map $f_0:\Omega_p \rightarrow \C{k}{n-2}{\lambda}\subset {\mathbb{P}}^{n}$, defined naturally by the embedding $\C{k}{n-2}{\lambda}\subset {\mathbb{P}}^{n}$, has the form $$ \displaystyle f_0(z)=[1:h_1(z^{k}):h_2(z^{k}): \cdots: h_{n-1}(z^{k}):z],$$ where $h_i(0)=\rho_{i}$.
nodes.statement_short: Write the embedding near $p$ as $[1:h_1(z^k):\cdots:h_{n-1}(z^k):z]$ with $h_i(0)=\rho_i$.

nodes.name: Push the parametrization down to $q=\pi(p)$ and note analyticity in $\lambda$
nodes.statement: By the construction, there exists a local chart $\zeta$ of $\C{k}{n-3}{\lambda}$ around the point $q:=\pi(p)$, and a local parametrization $$\tilde{f}_0:\Omega'_q\subset {\mathbb{C}}\rightarrow \C{k}{n-3}{\lambda}\subset {\mathbb{P}}^{n-1}:\zeta\mapsto \tilde{f}_0(\zeta)=[1:h_1(\zeta):h_2(\zeta): \cdots: h_{n-1}(\zeta)].$$ Recall that the morphism $\pi$ is defined in local charts as $\zeta=\pi(z)=z^k$. Additionally, if we consider a Taylor expansion of the $h_i(\zeta)$ we can observe that the coefficients are analytic functions in the variables $\lambda_1,...,\lambda_{n-2}$.
nodes.statement_short: The downstairs parametrization $\tilde{f}_0(\zeta)$ has Taylor coefficients analytic in the moduli parameters.

nodes.name: Local parametrization of $g_j$ at $q$
nodes.statement: Now let us consider the map $g_{j}:\C{k}{n-3}{\lambda}\rightarrow {\mathbb{P}}(Q(r-j))$. We note that, using the local parametrization of $\tilde{f}_0(\zeta)$ around the point $q$, a local parametrization of $g_{j}$ around the point $q$ can be found. Let $g_{j}(\zeta):=[1:h'_1(\zeta):\cdots:h'_{t_j}(\zeta)]$ be this local parametrization of $g_{j}$, where $t_j:=s(r-j)-1= \dim_{{\mathbb{C}}}Q(r-j)-1$. By construction the coefficients of $h'_i(\zeta)$ are analytic functions in the variables $\lambda_1,...,\lambda_{n-2}$.
nodes.statement_short: Transport the parametrization through $g_j$ to get $[1:h'_1(\zeta):\cdots:h'_{t_j}(\zeta)]$, again analytic in $\lambda$.

nodes.name: Build the Wronskian-type determinant $r(\lambda)$
nodes.statement: Given a formal series $l(\zeta)$, let $Tl$ be the vector column formed by all the coefficients of the formal series $l(\zeta)$ until the grade $t_j$. We consider the following analytic function defined over $\mathcal{P}_n$ $$r(\lambda_1,...,\lambda_{n-2})=\det(T1,Th'_1,...,Th'_{t_j}).$$
nodes.statement_short: Assemble truncated coefficient columns into an analytic determinant $r(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_{n-2})$.

nodes.name: Identify $\mho'_j$ with the non-vanishing locus of $r$
nodes.statement: Fixing the values $\lambda_1,...,\lambda_{n-2}$, the point $q\in \C{k}{n-3}{\lambda}$ is not a point of $\HC{j}{k}{n-3}{\lambda}$ if and only if $r(\lambda_1,...,\lambda_{n-2})$ is not zero. As $q'$ is not a point of $\HC{j}{k}{n-3}{\hat{\lambda}}$, we have that $r(\hat{\lambda}_1,...,\hat{\lambda}_{n-2})\neq 0$ (in particular, $r$ is not identically zero). The set $\mho'_j\subset \mathcal{P}_n$, where the analytic function $r$ does not vanish, is the sought after open set.
nodes.statement_short: $q$ is non-hyperosculating iff $r\neq0$; since $r(\hat\lambda)\neq0$, the non-vanishing locus is the desired open set.

nodes.name: Normal form of $g_j$ at $\pi(p)$ and the order inequalities $(\star)$
nodes.statement: Considering an automorphism of $ {\mathbb{P}}(Q(r-j))$, we can obtain the normal form of $g_j$ in $\pi(p)$: $$g_{j}(\zeta)=[1:g_{(1\; j)}(\zeta):g_{(2\;j)}(v):\cdots :g_{(t_j\;j)}(\zeta)],$$ where $t_j:=s(r-j)-1= \dim_{{\mathbb{C}}}Q(r-j)-1$, and the following inequalities are satisfied for each $0\leq j\leq r-1$: $$(\star) \left \{\begin{array}{lll} i\leq l_i:= {\mathrm{Ord}} g_{(i\; j)}(v),& \mbox{for all}& 1\leq i\leq t_j,\\ {\mathrm{Ord}} g_{(i\; j)}(v)< {\mathrm{Ord}} g_{(i+1\; j)}(v),& \mbox{for all} & i\geq 1. \end{array} \right.$$
nodes.statement_short: In normal form the orders $l_i={\mathrm{Ord}}\,g_{(i\,j)}$ satisfy $l_i\ge i$ and are strictly increasing.
conclusions: i\leq l_i:= {\mathrm{Ord}} g_{(i\; j)}(v),& \mbox{for all}& 1\leq i\leq t_j,
{\mathrm{Ord}} g_{(i\; j)}(v)< {\mathrm{Ord}} g_{(i+1\; j)}(v),& \mbox{for all} & i\geq 1.

nodes.name: When the orders satisfy $l_i=i$
nodes.statement: For fixed $j \in \{0, \ldots, r-1\}$ the equality $l_i=i$, $1\leq i\leq t_j$, is valid when $\pi(p)$ is not a hyperosculation point of the morphism $\C{k}{n-3}{\lambda}\rightarrow {\mathbb{P}}(Q(r-j))$.
nodes.statement_short: $l_i=i$ holds exactly when $\pi(p)$ is not hyperosculating for the morphism into ${\mathbb{P}}(Q(r-j))$.

nodes.name: Set up the two-case division
nodes.statement: The idea of the rest of the proof is to construct the normal form of the canonical embedding $f_c:\C{k}{n-2}{\lambda}\rightarrow {\mathbb{P}}^{g-1}$ in the point $p$ using the functions $g_{(i\; j)}$. We divide the proof into two cases: \begin{enumerate} \item[] {\bf Case 1:} $(n-1)(k-1)-2<k$. \item[] {\bf Case 2:} $(n-1)(k-1)-2\geq k$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Build the normal form of $f_c$ from the $g_{(i\,j)}$, splitting on whether $(n-1)(k-1)-2<k$.

nodes.name: Case 1: the small cases $(k,n)\in\{(2,4),(3,3)\}$
nodes.statement: {\bf Case 1:} Let us suppose that $(n-1)(k-1)-2<k$; that is $(k,n) \in \{(2,4),(3,3)\}$. In example \ref{ej:(2,4)} we have analyzed the case $(k,n)=(2,4)$. Let us consider a generalized Fermat curve $C^3(\lambda)$ of type $(3,3)$ and the morphism $\pi:C^3(\lambda)\rightarrow C^3$ , previously defined. Observe that $H^{0}(C^3(\lambda):\omega)\cong H^{0}(C^3(\lambda):\mathcal{O}(2))={\mathbb{C}}[x_0,x_1,x_2,x_3]_2$ (forms of degree $2$ of the polynomial ring ${\mathbb{C}}[x_0,x_1,x_2,x_3]$). Then, the canonical embedding $f_c$ is given by the following composition: \begin{center} $\xymatrix{ C^3(\lambda) \ar[r]_{f}\ar@/^1pc/[rr]^{f_c} &{\mathbb{P}}^{3}\ar[r]_{\nu_{2}}&{\mathbb{P}}^9} $. \end{center} Now let us consider the following morphism: \begin{center} $\xymatrix{ C^{3} \ar[r] \ar@/^1pc/[rr]^{g :=\nu_{2}\circ \tilde{f}_0}&{\mathbb{P}}^{2}\ar[r]&{\mathbb{P}}(Q(2))\cong {\mathbb{P}}^5}$, \end{center} where $Q(2)$ is the ${\mathbb{C}}$-vector space of Proposition \ref{pr:dim-s}, $\tilde{f}_0$ the natural embedding of $C^{3}$. Let us consider the normal form of $\tilde{f}_0$, and of $g$: \begin{center} $\tilde{f}_{0}(\zeta)=[1:\tilde{f}_{(0\;1)}(\zeta):\tilde{f}_{(0\;2)}(\zeta)]$, $g(\zeta)=[1:g_{1}(\zeta):g_{2}(\zeta):\cdots :g_{5}(\zeta)]$, \end{center} When $\pi(p)$ is not a hyperosculating point of $\tilde{f}_0:C^3\rightarrow {\mathbb{P}}^2$, we obtain that ${\mathrm{Ord}} \tilde{f}_{(0\;i)}(\zeta)=i$, $i\leq 2$. We also obtain that ${\mathrm{Ord}} g_{i}(\zeta)=i$, $i\leq 4$ and ${\mathrm{Ord}} g_{5}(\zeta)\geq 5$. Observe that ${\mathrm{Ord}} g_{5}(\zeta)=5$ if and only if $\pi(p)$ is not a hyperosculating point of the embedding $g:C^3\rightarrow {\mathbb{P}}^5$. As in this case, $\zeta:=\pi(z):=z^3$, if we define the functions \begin{center} $h_{i}(z):=\left \{ \begin{array}{ccc} g_{i}(z^3), & \mbox{if} & i=1,\\ z\tilde{f}_{(0\;1)}(z^3), & \mbox{if} & i=2,\\ g_2(z^3), & \mbox{if} & i=3,\\ \tilde{f}_{(0\;1)}(z^3)\tilde{f}_{(0\;2)}(z^3), & \mbox{if} & i=4,\\ g_{i-2}(z^3), & \mbox{if} & 5\leq i\leq 7, \end{array} \right.$ \end{center} then the normal form of the canonical embedding $f_c$ is given as $$f_{c}(z)=[1:z:z^2:h_1(z):\cdots :h_{7}(z)].$$ Additionally, we obtain $$a_i=i, \; 1\leq i\leq 5, \; a_6=7,\; a_7=8,\; a_8=10,\; a_9 = 13, \; a_{10} \geq 16,$$ so $\hat{w}(p)=14\leq w(p)$. The equality is fulfilled when $\pi(p)$ is not a hyperosculating point of the embedding $g:C^3\rightarrow {\mathbb{P}}^5$. The proof, for this situation, now follows from Lemma \ref{le:open-zariski}.
nodes.statement_short: Only $(2,4)$ and $(3,3)$ occur; for $(3,3)$ compute the gaps explicitly to get $\hat{w}(p)=14\le w(p)$.

nodes.name: Case 2: normal form of the canonical embedding via $h_{(i\,j)}$
nodes.statement: {\bf Case 2:} In the rest of we assume that $(n-1)(k-1)-2\geq k$, and we define the functions $$h_{(i\;j)}(z):=z^jg_{(i\;j)}(z^k),\; 0\leq j\leq k-1,\; 1\leq i \leq t_{j}.$$ Considering an automorphism of ${\mathbb{P}}^{g-1}$, where $g$ is the genus of $S$, we can suppose that the canonical embedding $f$ around the point $p$ is $$\tiny f(z):= [1:\cdots:z^{k-1}: h_{(1\;0)}(z):\cdots:h_{(1\;k-1)}(z):h_{(2\;0)}(z):\cdots: h_{(r\;k-2)}(z):$$$$:h_{(r+1\;0)}(z): \cdots:h_{(t_0\;0)}(z)],$$ where $r=t_{k-1}+1$.
nodes.statement_short: Define $h_{(i\,j)}(z)=z^jg_{(i\,j)}(z^k)$ and write the canonical embedding near $p$ in these coordinates.

nodes.name: Sum the order bounds and convert to the weight inequality
nodes.statement: Let $a_i$, $1\leq i\leq$ be the gap values of $p$. Since $ki+j\leq kl_i+j={\mathrm{Ord}} h_{(i\;j)}(z)$, $1\leq j \leq k-1$ and $1\leq i\leq t_j$, the following inequality is obtained $$\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}\sum_{i=0}^{t_{j}}(ki+j+1)\leq \sum_{i=1}^{g}a_{i}.$$ By Proposition \ref{pr:dim-s}, we have $$\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}\sum_{i=0}^{t_{j}}(ki+j+1)-\frac{g(g+1)}{2}=\frac{1}{24} (k-1) (k^{n-1}-2) (k^{n} + k^{n-1}-12),$$ from which we obtain the inequality part of the theorem, as the weight of the point $p$ is $$w(p):=\sum_{i=1}^{g}a_i-\frac{g(g+1)}{2}.$$
nodes.statement_short: From ${\mathrm{Ord}}\,h_{(i\,j)}\ge ki+j$ sum the gaps and subtract $g(g+1)/2$ to reach $\widehat{w}(p)$.

nodes.name: Conclude the equality part on the dense open set $\mho$
nodes.statement: As the set $\mho$ of the Lemma \ref{le:open-zariski} satisfies the condition of the previous remark, this finishes the proof of the last part of the theorem.
nodes.statement_short: The set $\mho$ meets the criterion of the previous remark, giving equality on a dense open set.

nodes.name: Equality criterion $w(p)=\hat{w}(p)$
nodes.statement: Observe that, for each $0\leq j\leq k-1$, $l_i=i$, for each $1\leq i\leq t_j$, if and only if $w(p)=\hat{w}(p)$. Combining this with Remark \ref{re:li=i} we obtain that $w(p)=\hat{w}(p)$ if and only if $\pi(p)$ is not a hyperosculating point of the morphism $\C{k}{n-3}{\lambda}\rightarrow {\mathbb{P}}(Q(r-j))$ for all $0\leq j\leq k-1$.
nodes.statement_short: $w(p)=\hat{w}(p)$ exactly when $\pi(p)$ is non-hyperosculating for every morphism $\C{k}{n-3}{\lambda}\to{\mathbb{P}}(Q(r-j))$.

nodes.name: Proof that the bound is not attained in the $C^5(-1)$ example
nodes.statement: Now we will verify that the bound of Theorem \ref{th:w-peso} is not achieved in Example \ref{ej:bound}. Consider the morphism $\pi: C^5(-1)\rightarrow C^5\; :[x_0:x_1:x_2:x_3]\rightarrow [x_0:x_1:x_2].$ As seen in the introduction $[1:1:-\sqrt[5]{2}]$ is a Weierstrass point of $C^5$, and in particular is a hyperosculating point of $C^5\rightarrow {\mathbb{P}}(Q(6))$, (this morphism is the canonical embedding). By virtue of Remark \ref{re:weie-weight} we obtain that $\hat{w}(p)<w(p)$.
nodes.statement_short: The image point is a Weierstrass point of $C^5$, hence hyperosculating, so the equality criterion fails and the bound is strict.

nodes.name: Introduce the covering $\pi:C^5(-1)\to C^5$
nodes.statement: Consider the morphism $\pi: C^5(-1)\rightarrow C^5\; :[x_0:x_1:x_2:x_3]\rightarrow [x_0:x_1:x_2].$
nodes.statement_short: Set up the degree-5 projection from $C^5(-1)$ onto the classic Fermat quintic.

nodes.name: The image point is hyperosculating for the canonical embedding of $C^5$
nodes.statement: As seen in the introduction $[1:1:-\sqrt[5]{2}]$ is a Weierstrass point of $C^5$, and in particular is a hyperosculating point of $C^5\rightarrow {\mathbb{P}}(Q(6))$, (this morphism is the canonical embedding).
nodes.statement_short: Leopoldt's Weierstrass point of $C^5$ is hyperosculating for $C^5\to{\mathbb{P}}(Q(6))$.

nodes.name: Apply the equality criterion to conclude strictness
nodes.statement: By virtue of Remark \ref{re:weie-weight} we obtain that $\hat{w}(p)<w(p)$.
nodes.statement_short: The equality criterion fails, so $\hat{w}(p)<w(p)$.
